A port on the Grand Canal and a big coal-mining area.
Q373023: Port city at the eastern tip of Shandong; the closest mainland Chinese city to South Korea.

Known as a clean coastal city and for sea cucumbers.
Q373101: Port city on the Yellow Sea in Shandong; the name means 'sunshine'.

Q37320: City in Ohio on the shore of Lake Erie.

Q3733: Capital of Guinea, on the Atlantic coast, originally on Tombo Island and the Kaloum Peninsula.
Founded as a French colonial capital in 1890.
A port that exports bauxite (aluminium ore), of which Guinea has the world's largest reserves.
About one in five Guineans live here.
Q373346: The largest prefecture-level city in Shandong by area and population.

Q373564: City in western Shandong on the Grand Canal.
Called the 'Venice of North China' for its lakes and canals; the Guangyue Tower is a landmark.

Q373687: City in northern Shandong on the Yellow River near its delta.
Hometown of Sun Tzu, author of 'The Art of War' (Huimin county).
A big textile and aluminium producer.
Q37400: Capital of Myanmar since 2005, a planned city built in secret by the military government.
Famous for very wide, mostly empty highways (up to 20 lanes).

Q374365: Saudi Arabia's second city and main port on the Red Sea.

Home of the King Fahd's Fountain, one of the tallest fountains in the world, and the Jeddah Formula 1 circuit.
Q3748: Capital of Liberia, on the Atlantic at Cape Mesurado.
Founded in 1822 by the American Colonization Society for freed Black Americans.
Named after US President James Monroe.
Heavily damaged during Liberia's civil wars (1989–2003).
Q3761: Capital of Ghana, on the Gulf of Guinea coast.

Q3766: Capital of Syria; often called the oldest continuously inhabited capital in the world.

Damascus steel and the damask fabric are named after the city.
Q376749: Bangladesh's second city and main seaport, on the Karnaphuli River near the Bay of Bengal.

An old trading port visited by Arab, Persian and Portuguese merchants.
Officially renamed Chattogram in 2018; gateway to the Chittagong Hill Tracts.
Q3777: Capital of Burkina Faso; often shortened to 'Ouaga'.
Traditional seat of the Mossi kings (Moro Naba), whose ceremony is still held every Friday.

Q3780: Capital of Sierra Leone, on one of the world's largest natural harbours.
Founded in 1792 as a home for freed slaves from Britain and the Americas, hence its name.

Q37836: The largest city in Wisconsin, on Lake Michigan.
Famous for beer brewing (Miller, Pabst, Schlitz), brought by German immigrants.
Home of Harley-Davidson motorcycles and its museum.
Hosts Summerfest, one of the largest music festivals in the world.
Q3787: Capital of Nigeria since 1991, a planned city in the centre of the country.
Chosen as a neutral site between the Muslim north and the Christian south, replacing Lagos.

Landmarks: the National Mosque and the National Christian Centre.
Q3792: Capital of Togo, on the Gulf of Guinea right at the border with Ghana.

Its deep-water port is one of the busiest in West Africa.
Known for the Akodessewa fetish market of voodoo items.
Q37951: Capital of Hokkaido, Japan's northernmost large island; Japan's fifth-largest city.

Q3799: Official capital of Benin, on a lagoon near the Nigerian border.

Capital of French Dahomey from 1900; most government offices are in Cotonou.
Known for its Afro-Brazilian architecture and the Great Mosque in Brazilian church style.
Q37995: Myanmar's largest city, formerly called Rangoon.
Capital until 2006, when the military government moved it to the new city of Naypyidaw.
The golden Shwedagon Pagoda is Myanmar's most sacred Buddhist site.
Has the largest number of British colonial-era buildings in Southeast Asia.
Q38022: City in Missouri near where the Missouri and Mississippi rivers meet.
Founded by French fur traders in 1764 and named after King Louis IX.

Hosted the 1904 World's Fair and Olympics; home of the blues and Budweiser beer.
Q3805: Capital of Jordan, originally built on seven hills.

Called Philadelphia in Greek and Roman times; a Roman theatre and the Citadel survive.
Grew from a small town after 1921 with waves of Palestinian, Iraqi and Syrian refugees.
Q3808: Capital of Cameroon, on seven hills in the centre of the country.
Founded in 1887 by German traders as a base for rubber and ivory.
Became capital of French Cameroon in 1922; Douala remains the larger economic city.
Known for the Reunification Monument and the Mvog-Betsi zoo.
Q3820: Capital of Lebanon, on a peninsula on the Mediterranean; inhabited for over 5,000 years.
Once called the 'Paris of the Middle East' for its cosmopolitan culture and banking.
Heavily damaged in the Lebanese Civil War (1975–1990).

Q3825: Capital of Gabon, on the Gabon Estuary near the equator.
Founded in 1849 by freed slaves from a captured slave ship; the name means 'free town' in French.
Grew rich with oil, manganese and timber exports.
Home to about a third of Gabon's people.
Q3826: Capital of Oman, on the Gulf of Oman with the Hajar Mountains behind it.
A trading port for centuries; held by the Portuguese in the 16th–17th centuries, whose forts Jalali and Mirani still stand.
Known for its low white buildings, the Muttrah corniche and souq, and the Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque.

Q38283: Japan's second-largest city, on Tokyo Bay south of Tokyo, in Kanagawa Prefecture.

Japan's first railway (1872) ran between Yokohama and Tokyo; hosted the 2002 FIFA World Cup final.
Q3832: Capital of the Central African Republic, on the Ubangi River opposite DR Congo.

Badly affected by civil conflict since 2013.
Q3838: Capital of DR Congo, on the Congo River directly across from Brazzaville, capital of the Republic of the Congo.

The largest French-speaking city in the world by population.
One of the fastest-growing megacities; the Rumble in the Jungle boxing fight (Ali vs Foreman) was held here in 1974.
Q3844: Capital of the Republic of the Congo, on the Congo River directly opposite Kinshasa.
Named after the explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, who founded it in 1880.

Q3854: Burundi's largest city and economic capital, on the northeastern shore of Lake Tanganyika.
Was the capital until 2019, when the government decided to move it to Gitega.
Ships most of Burundi's coffee and tea; began as a German military post called Usumbura.
Q38545: Turkey's fifth-largest city, on the Seyhan River near the Mediterranean.
Centre of the fertile Çukurova plain, famous for cotton.
Its Roman Stone Bridge (Taşköprü) is one of the oldest bridges in the world still in use.
Famous for the spicy Adana kebab.
Q3859: Capital of Rwanda, on rolling hills in the centre of the country.

Q59213: City in northern Guangdong on the Bei River; Guangdong's largest prefecture by area.

Q59218: Industrial city in the Pearl River Delta between Guangzhou and Shenzhen.
Known as 'the world's factory', a huge exporter of electronics, toys, textiles and furniture.
Home of the New South China Mall, one of the largest shopping malls in the world.
The 1839 burning of opium at Humen, a cause of the First Opium War, happened in Dongguan.
Q59223: City in the Pearl River Delta in Guangdong, between Guangzhou and Macau.
Named in 1925 after Sun Yat-sen (Sun Zhongshan), founding father of the Republic of China, who was born here.
His former residence in Cuiheng village is a museum.
A manufacturing centre for lighting, furniture and appliances.
Q59227: Historic city in eastern Guangdong, centre of the Teochew (Chaozhou) culture and dialect.
Ancestral home of millions of overseas Chinese in Southeast Asia, e.g. in Thailand and Singapore.
Known for Teochew cuisine, kung fu tea ceremony, and its ancient Guangji pontoon bridge.
Q597: Capital of Portugal on the Tagus estuary; one of the oldest cities in Western Europe.
Starting point of the Age of Discovery: Vasco da Gama sailed from here to India in 1497.
Largely destroyed by the 1755 earthquake and tsunami, then rebuilt in a grid by the Marquis of Pombal.
Known for its hills, yellow trams, Belém Tower, pastéis de nata and fado music.
Q5972: Capital of North Sumatra and Indonesia's largest city outside Java.
Grew in the late 19th century with Dutch tobacco plantations ('Deli tobacco').
Very diverse: Malay, Batak, Chinese, Javanese and Indian communities; the Maimun Palace was the sultan's residence.
Gateway to Lake Toba, the world's largest volcanic lake.
Q598985: City in Bihar on the north bank of the Ganges, in the Mithila region.
Kanwar Lake nearby is a Ramsar wetland and large bird sanctuary.
Has a big oil refinery (Barauni) and fertiliser and power plants.
Q60: The largest city in the USA, made of five boroughs: Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island.
Founded by the Dutch as New Amsterdam; renamed New York after the English took it in 1664.
Headquarters of the United Nations and home of Wall Street, the world's largest stock exchanges.
Landmarks: Statue of Liberty, Empire State Building, Central Park, Times Square.
Q604609: County-level city in Hunan under Zhuzhou.
Famous for underglaze porcelain; Mao Zedong's personal tableware came from Liling.
One of the birthplaces of fireworks, with Liuyang.
Q61: Capital of the United States, the District of Columbia, on the Potomac River between Maryland and Virginia.
Its site was chosen by George Washington; it became the capital in 1800, and the city plan was drawn by Pierre L'Enfant.
The White House, the Capitol and the Supreme Court are here.
The National Mall has the Lincoln Memorial, Washington Monument and the free Smithsonian museums.
Q6106: The largest city in Oregon, where the Willamette and Columbia rivers meet.
Its name was decided by a coin toss in 1845 (the other option was Boston).
Known for its bridges, food carts, Powell's bookshop and views of Mount Hood.
Headquarters of Nike is nearby in Beaverton.
Q612: The largest city of the United Arab Emirates, on the Persian Gulf coast.
Grew from a pearling village into a trade hub; oil, then tourism, trade and finance made it boom.
The Burj Khalifa (828 m) is the tallest building in the world; the Palm Jumeirah is an artificial island.
About 9 in 10 residents are foreign nationals.
Q61302: Capital of the Mexican state of Chihuahua.
Pancho Villa lived here; his house is now a museum of the Revolution.
Briefly capital of Mexico in 1864 under Benito Juárez during the French intervention.
Miguel Hidalgo, father of Mexican independence, was executed here in 1811.
Q61434: City on the Penna River in Andhra Pradesh.
Famous for its rice and Nellore cattle (which also became a key breed in Brazil).
Home of the Ranganatha temple and a big aquaculture (shrimp) industry.
Q62: City on a peninsula between the Pacific and San Francisco Bay, crossed by the Golden Gate Bridge.
Grew from a small settlement into a city during the California Gold Rush of 1849.
Largely destroyed by the 1906 earthquake and fire.
Known for cable cars, Alcatraz, Chinatown, LGBT history and the nearby Silicon Valley tech industry.
Q621001: Capital of Malanje Province in northern Angola, 380 km east of Luanda.
Near the Kalandula Falls, among the largest waterfalls in Africa by volume.
Also near the black rocks of Pungo Andongo and the habitat of the rare giant sable antelope.
Q622834: A railway junction on the main Delhi–Kolkata line.
Hometown of Nitish Kumar, long-time Chief Minister of Bihar; named after Bakhtiyar Khalji.
Q628: City in Lombardy at the foot of the Alps, north-east of Milan.
Its hilltop old town (Città Alta) is surrounded by Venetian walls that are a World Heritage Site.
Was one of the first and hardest-hit places in Europe in the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic.
Birthplace of the composer Gaetano Donizetti.
Q62823: Colombia's main Caribbean port, near the mouth of the Magdalena River.
Its Carnival is one of the biggest in the world and a UNESCO intangible heritage.
An entry point for immigrants and home of SCADTA (1919), one of the first airlines in the Americas; called the 'Golden Gate of Colombia'.
Q63139: The largest city of Cavite, south of Manila.
Grew rapidly as a commuter and university city with industrial parks.
Named after the Spanish governor Pérez Dasmariñas.
Q633036: The largest city of northeastern Thailand (Isan), also called Korat.
Gateway to the Isan region and Khao Yai National Park.
Its heroine Thao Suranari defended the city against Laos in 1826; her statue is the city's centre.
Phimai, a large Khmer temple, is nearby.
Q633530: City in West Bengal, headquarters of Murshidabad district.
Murshidabad, the last capital of independent Bengal's Nawabs, is nearby.
Was an early British East India Company cantonment; the 1857 rebellion's first stirrings were here.
Famous for silk and sweets like chhanabora.
Q6346: Capital of Indiana; nicknamed the 'Crossroads of America'.
Founded in 1821 as a planned capital in the centre of the state.
Hosts the Indianapolis 500, the largest single-day sporting event in the world, at its Motor Speedway.
Has more war memorials than any US city except Washington.
Q639421: Capital of the Union Territory of Puducherry on the Bay of Bengal.
The main town of French India until 1954; its French Quarter has yellow villas and French street names.
Home of the Sri Aurobindo Ashram; the experimental town Auroville is nearby.
Q6397066: Capital of Fars province in southwest Iran; called the city of poets, gardens and wine.
Burial place of the poets Hafez and Saadi, whose tombs are pilgrimage sites.
Capital of Iran under the Zand dynasty in the 18th century.
Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, is about 60 km away; the Pink Mosque is famous for its stained glass.
Q64: Capital of Germany on the Spree; the largest city in the European Union by population within city limits.
Divided by the Berlin Wall from 1961 until it fell in 1989; reunified as the capital in 1990.
Landmarks include the Brandenburg Gate, the Reichstag and Museum Island (a World Heritage Site).
Also one of Germany's 16 federal states.
Q643883: City in Punjab, Pakistan, near the border with Jammu.
Makes most of the world's hand-stitched footballs, as well as surgical instruments and sports goods.
Birthplace of the poet Muhammad Iqbal.
Ancient Sagala, capital of the Indo-Greek king Menander.
Q645725: City in the Mumbai metropolitan region, northeast of Thane.
Once called the 'Manchester of India' for its power-loom textile industry.
Today one of India's biggest warehouse and logistics hubs.
Q648: City in French Flanders near the Belgian border, capital of the Hauts-de-France region.
Was Flemish (Rijsel) until Louis XIV captured it in 1667; its Vauban citadel survives.
Hosts the Braderie, Europe's largest flea market, every September; connected to London and Brussels by Eurostar.
Q648298: Capital of Ituri Province in northeastern DR Congo, near Lake Albert.
Centre of the Ituri conflict between Hema and Lendu groups.
Hosts a large UN peacekeeping base; gold mining is nearby.
Q6487: City on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, the centre of the Turkish Riviera and the country's tourism capital.
Founded around 200 BC by King Attalus II of Pergamon as Attaleia.
Hadrian's Gate and the Kaleiçi old town survive; ancient Perge, Aspendos and Side are nearby.
Q649: Capital of Russia on the Moskva River; the largest city entirely in Europe.
First mentioned in 1147; the Grand Principality of Moscow unified the Russian lands.
Peter the Great moved the capital to Saint Petersburg in 1712; the Bolsheviks moved it back in 1918.
The Kremlin and Red Square with St Basil's Cathedral are World Heritage Sites; its Metro stations are famous for their decoration.
Q65: The second-largest city in the USA, in Southern California on the Pacific coast.
Centre of the global film and TV industry: Hollywood is a neighbourhood of the city.
Founded as a Spanish pueblo in 1781 and part of Mexico until 1848.
Known for sprawl and freeways; hosted the Summer Olympics in 1932 and 1984 and will again in 2028.
Q65061424: Greater Malang, the region around the city of Malang in East Java.
A cool highland area with many universities.
Includes Batu, a resort town known for apples and theme parks; gateway to Mount Bromo.
Q650908: Town in southwestern Central Java, capital of Banyumas Regency.
Sits at the foot of Mount Slamet, Java's second-highest volcano.
Known for the Banyumasan dialect and mendoan (half-fried tempeh).
Q651101: County-level city in Shandong under Weifang.
Hometown of Mo Yan, winner of the 2012 Nobel Prize in Literature, who set many stories here ('Red Sorghum').
Known for paper-cutting, clay toys and New Year prints (the 'three treasures').
Q656: Russia's second city, on the Neva River delta at the Baltic Sea; called Petrograd, then Leningrad (1924–1991).
Founded by Peter the Great in 1703 as Russia's 'window to Europe' and capital of the Russian Empire until 1918.
The October Revolution of 1917 began here; the city survived the 872-day Siege of Leningrad in WWII.
The Hermitage Museum in the Winter Palace is one of the largest museums in the world; known for its summer 'white nights'.
Q657072: Holy city of the Mouride Sufi brotherhood in central Senegal.
Founded in 1887 by Sheikh Ahmadou Bamba; his tomb is beside the Great Mosque (1963), one of Africa's largest.
The yearly Grand Magal pilgrimage draws millions.
Run by the brotherhood with special status: alcohol and tobacco are banned.
Q657428: Historic port city on Somalia's Indian Ocean coast, southwest of Mogadishu.
Capital of the Lower Shabelle region; home of the Bimal clan.
Known for its old coral-stone buildings.
Q657461: Port city on Colombia's Caribbean coast.
Founded in 1533; a key Spanish port for shipping silver to Spain and a major slave-trade port.
Its walled old city and fortresses (Castillo San Felipe) are a World Heritage Site.
Setting of many works by Gabriel García Márquez, who lived there.
Q659887: Town in central Kerala, called the 'City of Letters'.
Birthplace of major Malayalam newspapers like Malayala Manorama and Deepika.
The first town in India to reach 100% literacy (1989).
A centre of rubber plantations and Syrian Christian churches.
Q66485: Capital of Rajasthan, called the 'Pink City' for its pink-painted old town.
Founded in 1727 by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II as one of India's first planned cities; a World Heritage Site.
Landmarks: Hawa Mahal ('Palace of Winds'), City Palace, Jantar Mantar observatory and nearby Amber Fort.
Part of the 'Golden Triangle' tourist route with Delhi and Agra.
Q66568: Large industrial city in Uttar Pradesh on the Ganges; formerly called Cawnpore.
Site of the 1857 Siege of Cawnpore and massacre during the Indian Rebellion.
Once called the 'Manchester of the East' for its textile mills; also known for leather goods.
Home of IIT Kanpur, a leading engineering institute.
Q66616: The largest city of Madhya Pradesh, in central India.
Ruled by the Holkar dynasty of the Marathas; Queen Ahilyabai Holkar is still revered.
Ranked India's cleanest city in national surveys every year since 2017.
Famous for its street food, e.g. at Sarafa night market.
Q672672: Former capital of the Kingdom of Onattukara.
Has a large NTPC power plant and is a commercial centre of central Travancore.
Q6809876: Town in East Champaran district, northern Bihar.
Has a traditional industry making buttons from mother-of-pearl shells.
Q681198: University town in Enugu State, Nigeria.
Home of the University of Nigeria (1960), the first indigenous university in the country.
Near Igbo-Ukwu, where famous 9th-century bronzes were found, and the Opi iron-smelting site.
Q68481: Capital of Fujian, on the Min River estuary.
Called the 'Banyan City' for its many banyan trees.
One of the treaty ports opened after the First Opium War; its Three Lanes and Seven Alleys district is well preserved.
Origin of many overseas Chinese emigrants; known for Fuzhou fish balls and lacquerware.
Q68579: City in Fujian on the Taiwan Strait.
Birthplace of Mazu, the sea goddess worshipped across southern China and Taiwan; her temple is on Meizhou Island.
Known for longans and lychees, and for its many shoe factories.
Q68695: Port city in southern Fujian on the Taiwan Strait.
Known to medieval traders as Zaiton, it was one of the largest ports in the world; Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta praised it.
A World Heritage Site as an 'Emporium of the World', with Hindu, Muslim and Buddhist relics side by side.
Today a centre of shoe and sportswear makers (Anta, Xtep) in Jinjiang.
Q68744: Port city in Fujian on the Taiwan Strait, historically known as Amoy.
One of the treaty ports opened after the First Opium War; Gulangyu islet, with colonial villas, is a World Heritage Site.
One of China's first four Special Economic Zones (1980).
The Taiwanese-held Kinmen islands lie only a few kilometres offshore.
Q68814: City in southern Fujian, surrounding Xiamen together with Quanzhou.
Its Tulou — huge round earthen houses of the Hakka and Hokkien people — are partly a World Heritage Site.
Ancestral home of many Taiwanese and Southeast Asian Chinese families.
Known for narcissus flowers and pomelos.
Q68862: City in southwestern Fujian; the name means 'dragon rock'.
Its Hakka tulou earthen houses in Yongding are part of a World Heritage Site.
Gutian, where the Red Army held a famous 1929 conference, is in the area.
Q6905368: The municipality of Monterrey, capital of Nuevo León in northern Mexico.
Founded in 1596; the saddle-shaped Cerro de la Silla mountain is its symbol.
Mexico's main industrial city, home of Cemex and FEMSA (Coca-Cola bottler).
Q69060: Capital of Qinghai, the largest city on the Tibetan Plateau, at about 2,200 m.
An old Silk Road trading post; gateway to Tibet by the Qinghai–Tibet railway.
Near Kumbum (Ta'er) Monastery, birthplace of Tsongkhapa, founder of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism.
Its Dongguan Mosque is one of the largest in northwest China.
Q694939: Capital of Al-Qadisiyyah Governorate in southern-central Iraq.
Founded as a guesthouse of the Khaza'il tribe.
Centre of a rice and grain farming region on the Euphrates.
Q695623: Capital of Barinas state, the 'capital of the Llanos' plains in Venezuela.
Birthplace region of Hugo Chávez, whose family dominated state politics.
Centre of cattle ranching and llanero music.
Q699777: County-level city under Wenzhou, on Yueqing Bay in Zhejiang.
China's capital of low-voltage electrical products (e.g. Chint and Delixi in Liushi).
Much of the scenic Yandang Mountains lie in its area.
Q706161: County-level city in Zhejiang under Ningbo, on Hangzhou Bay.
A big centre of household appliance manufacturing.
The Hangzhou Bay Bridge connects it to the Shanghai area.
Q708605: Coastal new area of Tianjin on the Bohai Sea.
A major port and free-trade zone and site of the Tianjin Eco-City.
Site of the 2015 Tianjin explosions at a chemical warehouse that killed 173 people.
The Binhai Library is famous for its eye-shaped atrium.
Q71204: City in southeastern Hubei on the Yangtze.
An old mining centre: the Tonglüshan copper mine was worked 3,000 years ago.
The Hanyeping company here was China's first modern steel complex (1908).
Called the 'cradle of Chinese modern industry'.
Q71227: Home of Dongfeng Motor, which built its first truck factory here in 1969 — 'China's Car City'.
The Wudang Mountains, a Taoist sacred site and birthplace of Wudang kung fu, are in the prefecture.
Danjiangkou reservoir supplies water to Beijing through the South–North Water Transfer.
Q71247: City in southern Hubei on the Yangtze.
Its ancient name Jiangling was the capital of the Chu state; it has one of China's best-preserved city walls.
A key city in the Three Kingdoms story ('Guan Yu loses Jingzhou').
The Jingzhou Museum holds a 2,000-year-old preserved Han-dynasty body.
Q71266: City in western Hubei on the Yangtze, at the eastern end of the Three Gorges.
The Three Gorges Dam, the world's largest power station, and the Gezhouba Dam are here.
Birthplace of the poet Qu Yuan, honoured by the Dragon Boat Festival.
Was a key battle site in the Three Kingdoms period (Battle of Yiling).
Q71284: City in northwestern Hubei on the Han River, formed from Xiangyang and Fancheng.
Famous in the Three Kingdoms story; Zhuge Liang lived nearby.
The Siege of Xiangyang (1267–1273) by the Mongols was a turning point in the conquest of Song China.
Has one of the oldest intact city walls and widest moats in China.
Q71305: City in eastern Hubei on the Yangtze, next to Wuhan.
Was briefly the capital of the Wu state in the Three Kingdoms (as Wuchang).
Home of Ezhou Huahu Airport, Asia's first dedicated cargo hub airport (opened 2022).
Q713317: County-level city in Zhejiang under Taizhou.
Its Ming-dynasty city wall, the 'southern Great Wall', was built against pirates.
Has a well-preserved old street (Ziyang Street).
Q713357: County-level city under Wenzhou in Zhejiang.
A centre of private manufacturing, especially car parts.
Birthplace of Sun Yirang, a pioneer in reading the ancient oracle-bone script.
Q71339: City in Hubei northwest of Wuhan; the name means 'filial piety moves (heaven)'.
Named after the legend of Dong Yong, who sold himself to pay for his father's funeral.
Known for its rice-wine (mijiu) and sesame candy.
Q71468: City in central Hubei on the Jianghan Plain, west of Wuhan.
Hometown of Lu Yu, author of 'The Classic of Tea', honoured as the 'Sage of Tea'.
Has many emigrants and is known as a 'hometown of overseas Chinese'.
Q72: Switzerland's largest city, at the northern end of Lake Zurich.
A global financial centre with major banks and the Swiss stock exchange.
Home of ETH Zurich, where Einstein studied; the Dada art movement began here in 1916.
Often ranked one of the most liveable — and most expensive — cities in the world.
Q7253: Capital of West Sumatra on the Indian Ocean.
Centre of the Minangkabau people, known for their matrilineal culture and horn-shaped roofs.
Gave its name to Padang food, served across Indonesia (e.g. rendang).
Q7258412: Puebla, capital of the Mexican state of the same name, was founded by the Spanish in 1531 between Mexico City and Veracruz.
Its historic centre with colourful Talavera-tiled buildings is a World Heritage Site.
Origin of mole poblano sauce and chiles en nogada.
The Battle of Puebla (5 May 1862) against the French is the origin of Cinco de Mayo; the Great Pyramid of Cholula is nearby.
Q727: Capital of the Netherlands; the seat of government is The Hague.
Grew from a dam on the Amstel river into the world's leading trade port in the 17th-century Golden Age.
Its ring of canals (Grachtengordel) is a World Heritage Site.
Home of the Rijksmuseum, Van Gogh Museum and the Anne Frank House; more bicycles than people.
Q727731: Coastal town in Kanyakumari district, Tamil Nadu.
Site of the 1741 Battle of Colachel, where Travancore defeated the Dutch East India Company — a rare Asian victory over a European power.
A natural harbour where a new port is planned.
Q72778: Capital of Shanxi province, on the Fen River.
Over 2,500 years old and capital of several dynasties; nicknamed the 'Dragon City'.
A centre of coal mining, steel and heavy industry.
The Jinci Temple complex with its Song-dynasty halls is just outside the city.
Q72818: Vietnam's main northern port, on the Gulf of Tonkin; the third-largest city.
Nicknamed the 'City of Red Flamboyant Flowers'.
Includes Cát Bà Island, next to Hạ Long Bay.
Heavily bombed in the Vietnam War; home of VinFast car factory.
Q72877: City in northern Shanxi, near the Great Wall and Inner Mongolia.
Capital of the Northern Wei dynasty (as Pingcheng) in the 5th century.
The Yungang Grottoes, with 51,000 Buddhist statues, are a World Heritage Site; the Hanging Temple clings to a cliff nearby.
Q72907: Industrial city in eastern Shanxi at the foot of the Taihang Mountains.
A coal-mining centre known for anthracite.
Niangziguan pass of the Great Wall is nearby.
Q72945: City in southeastern Shanxi on the Shangdang plateau.
A strategic area in Chinese history, including the Battle of Changping (260 BC).
Important for coal and the Taihang Mountains scenery.
Q72990: City in southeastern Shanxi bordering Henan.
A coal-mining centre, known for anthracite and coalbed methane.
The Huangcheng Xiangfu castle of a Qing minister and the Wangmang Mountains are well known.
Q73045: City in central Shanxi, merged with Taiyuan into one urban area.
Includes Pingyao, a perfectly preserved Ming-dynasty walled town (World Heritage Site).
Home of the grand merchant family compounds, like the Qiao Family Compound.
Shanxi merchants from here founded China's first banks (piaohao).
Q73073: The southernmost city of Shanxi, near the Yellow River bend.
Built around the Yuncheng Salt Lake, which has supplied salt for over 4,000 years.
Hometown of Guan Yu, the Three Kingdoms general worshipped as a god; the Guandi Temple at Xiezhou is the largest of its kind.
The Stork Tower (Guanque Lou), famous in Tang poetry, is in the prefecture.
Q73156: City in southern Shanxi on the Fen River, called Pingyang in antiquity.
Traditionally the capital of the legendary Emperor Yao.
Was once called one of the world's most polluted cities because of coal mining.
The Hukou Waterfall on the Yellow River is in the prefecture.
Q738303: The largest city of Tamaulipas, on the Rio Grande opposite Hidalgo and McAllen, Texas.
One of the busiest border crossings for trade.
Q7449155: Residential town in northern Singapore on the Straits of Johor.
Was home to a major British naval base from the 1930s.
Has Singapore's only natural hot spring (Sembawang Hot Spring Park).
Q7473516: Capital of Japan and seat of the Emperor, at the head of Tokyo Bay on Honshu.
Originally called Edo; it became the seat of the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603 and was renamed Tokyo ('eastern capital') in 1868.
Governed as a prefecture-like 'Metropolis' with 23 special wards, including Shinjuku and Shibuya.
Hosted the Summer Olympics in 1964 and 2021.
Q74881: Port city at the southern tip of the Liaodong Peninsula in Liaoning.
Leased by Russia (as Dalny) and then held by Japan (as Dairen) from 1905 to 1945.
Its Lüshunkou district is the former Port Arthur, whose siege was the key battle of the Russo-Japanese War.
Known for its seaside parks, squares and summer Davos forum.
Q74957: Steel city in Liaoning, south of Shenyang; the name means 'saddle mountain'.
Home of Anshan Iron and Steel (Angang), one of China's biggest steelmakers.
Has a very large jade Buddha and the nearby Qianshan mountains.
Tanggangzi hot springs were a favourite of the last emperor Puyi.
Q75026: Industrial city in Liaoning on the Hun River, east of Shenyang.
Has one of the largest open-pit coal mines in Asia (West Open Pit Mine).
The last emperor Puyi was held in the Fushun War Criminals Management Centre for 'reeducation'.
Near Hetu Ala, the first capital of the Manchu leader Nurhaci.
Q75091: Steel and coal city in Liaoning, southeast of Shenyang.
Founded as a metallurgical centre in 1915; Benxi Steel was once China's fourth-largest steelmaker.
The 1942 Honkeiko colliery disaster here was the worst coal-mine accident in history.
Known for the Benxi Water Cave, a long underground river.
Q75110: The largest Chinese border city, on the Yalu River opposite Sinuiju, North Korea.
Most of China's trade with North Korea passes over its Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge.
The 'Broken Bridge' was bombed by the US in the Korean War; the Great Wall's eastern end (Hushan) is nearby.
Q75150: Port city in Liaoning on Liaodong Bay.
Opened as a treaty port (Newchwang) in 1861, the first in Northeast China.
Known for its hot springs at Xiongyue and magnesite mining.
Q75203: City in Liaoning on the Taizi River, south of Shenyang.
One of the oldest cities in Northeast China; Nurhaci's Later Jin made it a capital (1621–1625).
Its White Pagoda (Liao dynasty) is one of the tallest brick pagodas in the northeast.
Q75230: Coastal city in Liaoning on Liaodong Bay.
Built around the Liaohe oil field.
Famous for its Red Beach, where a seaweed turns the wetlands bright red in autumn.
Known for rice and river crabs.
Q75379: Coastal city in western Liaoning; the name means 'gourd island'.
Includes Xingcheng, a well-preserved Ming walled town.
Q7563836: Large township 30 km north of Pretoria.
Its name is an acronym of Sotho, Shangaan, Nguni and Venda, the groups placed there under apartheid.
Part of the City of Tshwane.
Q7567412: The conurbation of Portsmouth and Southampton on England's south coast, sometimes called 'Solent City'.
Portsmouth is the home of the Royal Navy with HMS Victory; Southampton is a major cruise port.
The Titanic sailed from Southampton in 1912.
Includes Gosport, Fareham, Havant and Eastleigh.
Q7568: City in south-central Java, the only Indonesian region still ruled by a sultan (also its governor).
Served as Indonesia's capital in 1946–48 during the war of independence.
A centre of Javanese culture: batik, gamelan and wayang puppetry.
Gateway to the Borobudur and Prambanan temples; home of Gadjah Mada University.
Q7578: Jambi is the capital of Jambi province on the Batang Hari River in Sumatra.
Near the Muaro Jambi temple complex, one of the largest ancient Buddhist sites in Southeast Asia.
Was part of the Malayu and Srivijaya kingdoms; today a centre of rubber and palm oil.
Q760714: Bihar's third city, on the Ganges.
Called the 'Silk City' for its tussar silk.
Near the ruins of Vikramashila, a great Buddhist university of the Pala era.
The river here has a sanctuary for the endangered Ganges river dolphin.
Q765487: Town in Fars province, about 80 km southeast of Shiraz.
Its Sasanian palace (5th century) is part of a World Heritage Site.
Known for its yoghurt and olive and pistachio farming.
Q768864: City just north of Bangkok, Thailand's second-largest city municipality.
Grew as a suburb of Bangkok along the Chao Phraya River.
Known for its durian orchards and Ko Kret island with Mon pottery villages.
Q7786: Capital of Riau province on the Siak River in Sumatra; the name means 'new market'.
Centre of Indonesia's oil (the Minas field) and palm oil industries.
Riau Malay culture: the Siak Sultanate palace is nearby.
Q7880: France's fourth city, on the Garonne in the southwest.
Called the 'Pink City' for its brick buildings; the Basilica of Saint-Sernin is a World Heritage Site.
Europe's aerospace capital: headquarters of Airbus and a big space centre.
Capital of the Visigothic Kingdom in the 5th century; known for rugby and cassoulet.
Q7903: Morocco's largest city and economic centre, on the Atlantic coast.
The Hassan II Mosque has one of the tallest minarets in the world (210 m), partly built over the sea.
Developed by the French as the main port of their protectorate from 1912; known for Art Deco buildings.
Gave its name to the 1942 film 'Casablanca'; hosted the 1943 Allied conference.
Q795595: Provincial capital in southern Thailand, on Songkhla Lake near Malaysia.
Forms a metro area with Hat Yai, the region's commercial centre.
Known for Samila Beach and its golden mermaid statue.
An old port with Chinese and Malay influences.
Q79857: City on the Central Anatolian Plateau in Turkey; called Iconium in antiquity.
Capital of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in the Middle Ages.
The poet Rumi lived and is buried here; it is the home of the Mevlevi 'whirling dervishes'.
Çatalhöyük, one of the oldest towns in the world (about 9,000 years old), is nearby.
Q7986320: The western part of the Witwatersrand, west of Johannesburg.
Settled after gold was found in 1886; includes Krugersdorp, Randfontein and Roodepoort.
Near the Cradle of Humankind fossil sites (World Heritage Site).
Q79867: The largest metro area in Alabama.
Founded in 1871 and named after Birmingham, England; grew as a steel city ('Magic City').
A centre of the civil rights movement: the 1963 Birmingham campaign and the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing.
Its Vulcan statue is the largest cast-iron statue in the world.
Q79980: Holy Hindu city on the Ganges in Uttar Pradesh, also called Benares or Kashi; one of the oldest inhabited cities in the world.
Pilgrims bathe at its riverside ghats; Hindus believe dying here brings release from rebirth, so cremations burn at Manikarnika Ghat.
The Buddha gave his first sermon at nearby Sarnath.
Known for Banarasi silk saris and Hindustani classical music.
Q80053: Capital of East Azerbaijan in northwest Iran; Iran's main Azerbaijani (Turkic) city.
Its historic bazaar is one of the largest covered bazaars in the world (World Heritage Site).
Was a capital of several Persian dynasties, incl. the Ilkhanate and early Safavids.
Q804027: Metropolitan region on the coast of São Paulo state, centred on Santos.
The Port of Santos is the busiest container port in Latin America.
Santos is home of Pelé's club, Santos FC; Cubatão is a big industrial hub.
A popular beach area for São Paulo residents.
Q80484: Capital of Bihar on the south bank of the Ganges.
As Pataliputra it was the capital of the Maurya Empire under Ashoka and of the Gupta Empire.
Birthplace of the tenth Sikh Guru, Gobind Singh; Bodh Gaya and Nalanda are nearby.
One of the oldest continuously inhabited places in the world.
Q80985: City in northern Morocco, the country's spiritual and cultural capital.
Founded in the 8th century; the University of al-Qarawiyyin (859) is often called the oldest existing university in the world.
Its medina, Fes el-Bali, is one of the largest car-free urban areas in the world (World Heritage Site).
Famous for its leather tanneries; the fez hat is named after it.
Q80989: Capital of Madhya Pradesh, called the 'City of Lakes' for its Upper and Lower Lakes.
Ruled by a line of female rulers, the Begums of Bhopal, in the 19th and early 20th centuries.
The 1984 Bhopal gas disaster at a Union Carbide pesticide plant was the world's worst industrial disaster.
The Buddhist stupas of Sanchi and the prehistoric rock shelters of Bhimbetka are nearby.
Q81033: Capital of Nuevo León and Mexico's main industrial city, at the foot of the Sierra Madre Oriental.
Founded in 1596; the saddle-shaped Cerro de la Silla mountain is its symbol.
Headquarters of big companies like Cemex and FEMSA; close ties with Texas.
Known for cabrito (roast goat) and the Fundidora steelworks turned into a park.
Q8131: Capital of South Sumatra, on both banks of the Musi River.
Centre of the Srivijaya empire, a Buddhist maritime power in the 7th–13th centuries.
The Ampera Bridge is its symbol.
Famous for pempek fish cakes and co-hosted the 2018 Asian Games.
Q81398: Port and resort city on Mexico's Pacific coast in Guerrero.
From 1565 the Manila galleons sailed between Acapulco and the Philippines for 250 years.
A glamorous resort of Hollywood stars in the 1950s–60s; famous for the La Quebrada cliff divers.
Badly damaged by Hurricane Otis in 2023.
Q8156: Capital of Lampung province at the southern tip of Sumatra.
The main gateway between Sumatra and Java via the Bakauheni ferry across the Sunda Strait.
Hit by the tsunami from the 1883 Krakatoa eruption; the volcano lies offshore.
A centre of coffee, pepper and tapioca trade.
Q817269: City in North Kivu, eastern DR Congo, near the Virunga National Park and the Rwenzori Mountains.
A trading centre on the edge of the Ituri rainforest.
Has suffered from armed group violence and Ebola outbreaks.
Q81788: City on the west bank of the Nile opposite Cairo, part of Greater Cairo.
Home of the Great Pyramid of Khufu, the only surviving one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and the Great Sphinx.
The Grand Egyptian Museum, the world's largest archaeological museum, opened near the pyramids.
Ancient Memphis, Egypt's first capital, lies a little to the south.
Q81882: Port city on São Vicente island in São Paulo state.
Its port is the busiest in Latin America and once set world coffee prices (Coffee Museum).
Home of Santos FC, where Pelé played; Pelé's memorial and tomb are here.
Has the world's longest beachfront garden (Guinness).
Q83061: City in eastern Turkey on the shore of Lake Van, Turkey's largest lake.
As Tushpa it was the capital of the Urartu kingdom (9th–6th centuries BC); the Van Fortress survives.
Famous for the Van cat with odd-coloured eyes, and for its breakfasts.
Akdamar Island in the lake has a 10th-century Armenian church.
Q83114: Municipality in Rio de Janeiro state, across Guanabara Bay from Rio.
The second most populous municipality in the state.
Mostly a working-class commuter city, next to Niterói.
Q83189: Capital of Goiás in central Brazil, a planned city founded in 1933.
Has a large collection of Art Deco buildings.
Known for its parks and green spaces and for sertanejo country music.
The 1987 Goiânia radiation accident with a stolen caesium-137 source was one of the worst ever.
Q83317: Iraq's second city, on the Tigris in the north.
Opposite the ruins of Nineveh, capital of the Assyrian Empire and once the largest city in the world.
Gave its name to muslin cloth.
Held by ISIS from 2014 to 2017; its Great Mosque of al-Nuri was destroyed and is being rebuilt.
Q83387: The largest Kurdish-majority city in Turkey, on the Tigris River.
Its massive black basalt city walls (about 6 km long) are among the longest in the world; with the Hevsel Gardens a World Heritage Site.
Inhabited for about 10,000 years; called Amida in antiquity.
Q836527: City in western Tamil Nadu, the 'Knitwear Capital of India'.
Exports cotton knitwear and T-shirts to brands around the world.
Lies on the Noyyal River, which has suffered from dyeing pollution.
Q837425: Second city of Xinjiang, seat of Bayingolin Mongol Prefecture, China's largest prefecture.
A base of the Tarim Basin oil fields; Bosten Lake is nearby.
Q838785: City in Riverside County, California, part of the Temecula–Murrieta area.
Known for the Temecula Valley wine country and its Old Town.
Has the Pechanga Resort Casino of the Pechanga Band of Luiseño Indians nearby.
Q84: Capital of the United Kingdom, on the River Thames; the largest metro area in Western Europe.
Founded by the Romans as Londinium; the medieval 'City of London' is now the financial district.
In the 19th century it was the largest city in the world, capital of the British Empire.
Big Ben, the Tower of London, Buckingham Palace; the only city to have hosted three Summer Olympics (1908, 1948, 2012).
Q842411: Twin city of Ayodhya on the Saryu River, Uttar Pradesh.
The first capital of the Nawabs of Awadh, with the tomb of Bahu Begum and the Gulab Bari garden.
Next to Ayodhya, the birthplace of Rama and site of the new Ram temple (2024).
Q85: Capital of Egypt near the Nile Delta; Greater Cairo is the largest urban area in Africa and the Arab world.
The Giza pyramids and ancient Memphis lie within the metropolitan area.
Founded in 969 by the Fatimids; called 'the city of a thousand minarets', its historic centre is a World Heritage Site.
Home to Al-Azhar University, one of the oldest universities in the world.
Q851576: Capital of South Darfur in western Sudan.
The name means 'place of chatting' in the Daju language.
A trading centre and railway terminus for western Sudan; deeply affected by the Darfur conflicts.
Q852238: Port city on the east bank of the Niger River in Anambra State, Nigeria.
Its Onitsha Main Market is one of the largest markets in West Africa.
A major Igbo trading centre, connected to Asaba by the Niger Bridge.
Known for 'Onitsha market literature', cheap pamphlet novels popular from the 1940s to 1960s.
Q855997: City in central Punjab, Pakistan; one of the country's planned cities.
Called the 'City of Eagles' for its large Pakistan Air Force base.
A big citrus-growing area famous for kinnow mandarins.
Q856003: Royal city of Selangor, Malaysia, on the Klang River west of Kuala Lumpur.
The old capital of Selangor; still seat of the Sultan's palace.
Next to Port Klang, Malaysia's busiest port.
Famous for bak kut teh (pork rib soup).
Q85751443: Administrative centre of Chandanaish Upazila, south of Chittagong.
Q8646: A special administrative region of China on the south coast, made of Hong Kong Island, Kowloon and the New Territories.
British colony from 1841 (after the First Opium War) until the handover to China in 1997; governed under 'one country, two systems'.
One of the world's leading financial centres, with the world's largest number of skyscrapers.
Victoria Harbour, the Peak and dim sum are icons; Cantonese and English are official.
Q8652: Coastal city in South Florida on Biscayne Bay; its metro area includes Fort Lauderdale and West Palm Beach.
About 70% of residents are Hispanic; Cuban exiles shaped neighbourhoods like Little Havana.
Known as the 'Capital of Latin America' for banking and trade, and for Miami Beach's Art Deco district.
Its port is the world's busiest cruise port.
Q8660: Capital of Sindh and Pakistan's largest city and main seaport, on the Arabian Sea.
Founded as the fishing village of Kolachi in 1729; it grew huge with refugees after the 1947 partition.
Birthplace of Pakistan's founder Muhammad Ali Jinnah, whose mausoleum is a city landmark.
Q8673: Nigeria's largest city and Africa's most populous urban area, on a lagoon on the Gulf of Guinea.
Capital of Nigeria until 1991, when the government moved to Abuja.
West Africa's financial centre; handles most of Nigeria's exports through its ports.
Centre of Nollywood films and Afrobeats music; the Yoruba name for the city is Èkó.
Q8678: Brazil's second-largest city, between mountains and the Atlantic; nicknamed the 'Marvellous City'.
Capital of Brazil until 1960 (when Brasília took over); from 1808 to 1821 it was also seat of the Portuguese royal court.
Christ the Redeemer statue, Sugarloaf Mountain, Copacabana and Ipanema beaches.
Famous for its Carnival and samba; hosted the 2016 Summer Olympics; residents are called cariocas.
Q868203: Capital of Osun State in southwestern Nigeria.
The Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove, a forest of shrines and sculptures to the river goddess Osun, is a World Heritage Site.
The yearly Osun-Osogbo festival draws pilgrims from around the world.
Austrian artist Susanne Wenger helped restore the grove.
Q8684: Capital of South Korea on the Han River; half of the country's people live in the Seoul metropolitan area.
Capital of the Joseon dynasty for over 500 years, surrounded by the Fortress Wall of Seoul.
Changed hands four times in the Korean War and was rebuilt during the 'Miracle on the Han River'.
Headquarters of Samsung and a centre of K-pop; hosted the 1988 Summer Olympics.
Q8686: China's largest city, on the Yangtze estuary, split by the Huangpu River into Puxi and the Pudong skyscraper district.
Its port is the busiest container port in the world.
Opened as a treaty port after the First Opium War (1842); the foreign concessions made it Asia's financial hub in the 1930s.
The Bund waterfront has a row of colonial-era banks and trading houses.
Q868631: Sindh's third city, on the Indus opposite Rohri.
The Sukkur Barrage (1932) feeds one of the world's largest irrigation systems.
The Lansdowne Bridge and the island temple of Sadh Belo are landmarks.
Q87: Egypt's second city and main port, on the Mediterranean at the western edge of the Nile Delta.
Founded in 331 BC by Alexander the Great; capital of Ptolemaic Egypt and of Cleopatra.
Its ancient Lighthouse (Pharos) was one of the Seven Wonders, and its Great Library the biggest of antiquity.
The modern Bibliotheca Alexandrina revives the library.
Q875070: City on Lingayen Gulf in Pangasinan, Philippines.
Famous for bangus (milkfish), celebrated with a yearly Bangus Festival.
Badly hit by the 1990 Luzon earthquake.
Q8818: Spain's third city, on the Mediterranean, capital of the Valencian Community.
Founded by the Romans in 138 BC; its cathedral claims to hold the Holy Grail.
Home of paella and the Las Fallas festival, where giant figures are burned in March.
The City of Arts and Sciences by Santiago Calatrava lies in the old riverbed of the Turia.
Q883: Russia's third-largest city and the largest in Siberia, on the Ob River.
Founded in 1893 where the Trans-Siberian Railway crossed the Ob.
Akademgorodok, a science town, is a major Russian research centre.
Has one of the largest opera and ballet theatres in Russia.
Q887: Russia's fourth-largest city, in the Urals at the border of Europe and Asia.
Founded in 1723 and named after Empress Catherine I; called Sverdlovsk in Soviet times (1924–1991).
The last Tsar Nicholas II and his family were executed here in 1918.
Birthplace of Boris Yeltsin; a big industrial centre.
Q888418: Town in Fars province, southern Iran.
Capital of Kavar County in a farming region southeast of Shiraz.
Q888665: Municipality in Alappuzha district, Kerala, south of Kochi.
Lies in the coir and backwater region of Kerala.
Known for the Cherthala Karthyayani temple.
Q888794: Town in Fars province, about 80 km east of Shiraz.
Lies near Lake Bakhtegan and Lake Tashk, important wetlands for flamingos.
Q891: City at the confluence of the Volga and Oka rivers; called Gorky from 1932 to 1990.
Founded in 1221; its Kremlin overlooks the rivers.
A big industrial centre (GAZ cars); was closed to foreigners in Soviet times — Andrei Sakharov was exiled here.
Birthplace of writer Maxim Gorky; hosted 2018 World Cup matches.
Q894: City on the Volga in Russia; called Kuybyshev from 1935 to 1991.
In WWII it was the planned backup capital: Stalin had a deep bunker built here.
A centre of the space industry: it built the rockets for Gagarin's flight.
Famous for its long Volga embankment and Zhiguli beer.
Q8969: The largest city of Quintana Roo, on the Caribbean coast of the Yucatán Peninsula.
Built from scratch as a planned tourist resort since 1970.
Its Hotel Zone lies on a narrow strip of sand between the sea and a lagoon.
Gateway to the Riviera Maya, Tulum and Chichén Itzá.
Q897320: City in eastern Bangladesh, one of the country's oldest municipalities (1868).
Its Titas gas field is the largest natural gas field in Bangladesh.
Known as the hometown of many famous musicians, e.g. Alauddin Khan, teacher of Ravi Shankar.
Q898: Siberian city on the Irtysh River, a stop on the Trans-Siberian Railway.
Dostoevsky was imprisoned here in a labour camp (1850–54).
Capital of Admiral Kolchak's anti-Bolshevik White government in 1918–1920, which held the imperial gold reserve.
Q90: Capital of France on the Seine, nicknamed the 'City of Light'.
Divided into 20 arrondissements; Haussmann's 19th-century boulevards shaped the modern city.
The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum; other landmarks are the Eiffel Tower and Notre-Dame.
Hosted the Summer Olympics in 1900, 1924 and 2024.
Q900: Capital of Tatarstan, on the Volga; a meeting point of Russian and Tatar cultures.
Capital of the Kazan Khanate until Ivan the Terrible conquered it in 1552.
Its Kremlin, with the Qolşärif Mosque and an Orthodox cathedral side by side, is a World Heritage Site.
Tolstoy and Lenin studied at its university; calls itself Russia's 'third capital'.
Q9022: Capital of Jalisco and Mexico's second-largest metro area; nicknamed the 'Pearl of the West'.
Founded in 1542 by the Spanish and named after Guadalajara in Spain.
Considered the birthplace of mariachi music and tequila (the town of Tequila is nearby).
A tech hub called the 'Mexican Silicon Valley'.
Q906: Industrial city on the eastern side of the southern Urals.
Called 'Tankograd' in WWII for its tank factories.
A meteor exploded over the city in February 2013, injuring about 1,500 people.
The ancient Bronze Age settlement Arkaim is in the region.
Q908: Port city on the Don River in southern Russia, near the Sea of Azov.
Founded in 1749 as a customs post; grew as a grain-trading centre.
Hosted 2018 World Cup matches; headquarters of Russia's Southern Military District.
Q911: Capital of Bashkortostan, at the confluence of the Belaya and Ufa rivers.
Founded in 1574 as a fortress under Ivan the Terrible.
A centre of oil refining and chemicals.
The statue of Salawat Yulayev, Bashkir national hero, overlooks the river.
Q914: City on the Volga in southern Russia; called Tsaritsyn until 1925 and Stalingrad from 1925 to 1961.
The Battle of Stalingrad (1942–43) was a turning point of WWII and one of the bloodiest battles in history.
The Motherland Calls statue on Mamayev Kurgan is one of the tallest statues in the world.
Stretches about 80 km along the Volga.
Q915: City on the Kama River near the Ural Mountains.
Near the Perm-36 Gulag camp museum and the Kungur Ice Cave.
A centre of oil, chemicals and aircraft engines; associated with the setting of Pasternak's 'Doctor Zhivago'.
Q919: City in Siberia on the Yenisei River.
Anton Chekhov called it the most beautiful city in Siberia; it appears on the 10-ruble note.
One of the largest aluminium producers in Russia.
Near the Stolby nature reserve with its rock pillars.
Q92161: Capital of Jilin province in Northeast China; the name means 'long spring'.
As Hsinking ('new capital') it was the capital of the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo (1932–1945).
Puyi, the last emperor of China, lived in its Imperial Palace of Manchukuo.
China's 'automobile city': home of FAW, the first Chinese carmaker, and a film studio.
Q92277: Jilin City, in China's northeast, lies on the Songhua River and was the original capital of Jilin province.
The only major Chinese city that shares its name with its province.
Famous for 'rime ice' (wusong): trees along the river coated in white frost in winter.
Q92348: City in southeastern Jilin bordering North Korea; the name means 'White Mountain'.
Named after Changbai Mountain (Paektu), with its crater lake Heaven Lake.
Known for mineral water springs and ginseng.
Q9248: Capital of Azerbaijan on the Caspian Sea; at 28 m below sea level, the lowest-lying capital in the world.
An early centre of the oil industry: around 1900 it produced half of the world's oil.
Its walled old city with the Maiden Tower and the Palace of the Shirvanshahs is a World Heritage Site.
Known for the modern Flame Towers and the Heydar Aliyev Center by Zaha Hadid.
Q925293: County-level city in Jiangsu under Zhenjiang.
The world's biggest centre of eyeglass lenses: about half of all lenses are made here.
Known for Southern Dynasties royal tomb sculptures (stone qilin).
Q929062: City in northern Punjab, Pakistan, on the Chenab River.
Part of the 'Golden Triangle' of industry with Sialkot and Gujranwala; known for fans and furniture.
Setting of the folk romance of Sohni Mahiwal.
The 1849 Battle of Gujrat ended the Sikh Empire.
Q93230: City in Punjab, Pakistan, next to Islamabad — together called the 'twin cities'.
Grew as the largest British army garrison town in northern India after 1849.
The ancient Gandhara city of Taxila, a World Heritage Site, is nearby.
Q93338: City in south-central Turkey, called Aintab or Antep historically, about 100 km north of Aleppo.
Famous as the baklava and pistachio capital of Turkey and a UNESCO City of Gastronomy.
The Zeugma Mosaic Museum holds one of the largest collections of Roman mosaics, including the 'Gypsy Girl'.
Badly hit by the 2023 Turkey–Syria earthquakes.
Q9361: Capital of Kyrgyzstan, at the foot of the Tian Shan mountains near Kazakhstan.
Grew from a Kokand fortress (Pishpek); called Frunze in Soviet times (1926–1991).
Has wide tree-lined Soviet boulevards and the Ala-Too Square.
Known for its bazaars, like Osh Bazaar.
Q9365: Capital of Tajikistan, in the Hisar Valley.
Grew from a village with a Monday market — 'Dushanbe' means Monday in Tajik.
Has one of the world's tallest flagpoles and a huge teahouse and national library.
Q955745: Municipality of El Alto, Bolivia's second-largest city, on the Altiplano above La Paz at about 4,100 m.
One of the highest big cities in the world; home to La Paz's international airport.
Mostly Aymara; known for its colourful 'cholet' buildings and a huge Thursday/Sunday market.
Q956: Capital of China, formerly romanized as Peking; the world's most populous national capital.
Seat of emperors of the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties: the Forbidden City and Temple of Heaven are World Heritage Sites.
The Great Wall passes through the mountains north of the city.
The only city to have hosted both the Summer (2008) and Winter (2022) Olympics.
Q956602: City in Chhattisgarh, forming one urban area with Bhilai.
Bhilai is home to the Bhilai Steel Plant, built with Soviet help in the 1950s, India's main producer of rails.
Second-largest urban area of the state after Raipur.
Q956893: Town in northern Kerala, centre of a large urban agglomeration of towns and villages.
Headquarters of Malappuram district, the most populous district in Kerala.
Has close ties with the Gulf states through migrant workers.
Associated with the 1921 Malabar Rebellion against British rule.
Q963782: County-level city in Guangxi under Guigang.
Jintian village here is where Hong Xiuquan launched the Taiping Rebellion in 1851.
Known for Xishan tea and the Xishan scenic mountain.
Q975: Home of the Alamo, the mission where Texan defenders were killed by Mexican troops in 1836 ('Remember the Alamo!').
Its five Spanish missions are a World Heritage Site; the River Walk follows the river through downtown.
Known for Tex-Mex food and a majority Hispanic population.
Q9824: City in Tamil Nadu on the Kaveri River.
Called the 'Turmeric City': one of the world's largest turmeric markets.
Also a big textile and handloom trade centre.
Hometown of the social reformer Periyar E. V. Ramasamy.
Q9863: City in Tamil Nadu surrounded by the Eastern Ghats.
Has India's largest magnesite deposits and the Salem Steel Plant.
Famous for mangoes and sago (tapioca) production.
Gateway to the Yercaud hill station.
Q987: Capital of India and seat of all three branches of government, inside the larger city of Delhi.
Designed by British architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker; the foundation stone was laid by George V in 1911.
Inaugurated as the capital of British India in 1931, replacing Calcutta.
Q9885: Tamil Nadu's second city, at the foot of the Western Ghats; called the 'Manchester of South India' for its textile mills.
Lies at the Palakkad Gap, the old trade route between Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Known for pumps, motors and engineering industries.
Gateway to the hill station Ooty and the Isha Foundation's giant Adiyogi Shiva statue.
Q993859: The second-largest city of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, in the Peshawar Valley.
The Ashoka rock edicts at Shahbaz Garhi (3rd century BC) are among the earliest writing in South Asia.
The Takht-i-Bahi Buddhist monastery nearby is a World Heritage Site.
Home of the Guides regiment of the British Indian Army.
Q994: Capital of Georgia, on the Kura River in the Caucasus.
Founded in the 5th century by King Vakhtang I; the name comes from 'warm' for its sulphur hot springs.
Its old town has sulphur bathhouses, the Narikala fortress and colourful balconied houses.
Seat of the Russian Caucasus Viceroyalty from 1801 to 1917.
Q994085: Capital of Kogi State, at the confluence of the Niger and Benue rivers.
Founded in 1857 by the explorer William Balfour Baikie as a trading post.
Was the first administrative capital of the British Northern Nigeria Protectorate; Lord Lugard's house survives.
The name 'Nigeria' was coined by Flora Shaw, Lugard's wife.
Q99648: City in the green highlands of Yemen; the capital of Ibb Governorate.
Called the 'fertile province' for its terraced fields and high rainfall.
Jibla, an old capital of Queen Arwa, is nearby.
